title: The Shor Code
summary: Shor's nine-qubit code concatenates the phase-flip and bit-flip codes and corrects an arbitrary error on one qubit.
objectives: Build the nine-qubit Shor code by encoding the phase-flip code with the bit-flip code
Decode with a majority vote inside each block and then across the block leaders
Explain why correcting X, Y and Z on one qubit also corrects an arbitrary error on that qubit
Tell which two-qubit errors the code corrects and which it turns into a logical error
mission: A real error is rarely a clean X or Z, so the code has to cover every error on one qubit. Complete encode(): a phase-flip code on the block leaders 0, 3 and 6, then a bit-flip code inside each block (0, 1, 2), (3, 4, 5) and (6, 7, 8). Complete decode(): undo the bit-flip codes with a majority vote in each block, then undo the phase-flip code with a majority vote on the leaders. Afterwards qubit 0 must hold the input state again after an X, Y or Z error on any one of the nine qubits, and after an arbitrary rotation on any one qubit, for any input state.

prediction.question: Z errors hit qubits 0 and 1, both in the first block. What happens to the decoded qubit 0?
options: A logical X, as for Z on qubits 0 and 3 in different blocks
A logical Z: two errors in one block beat the inner vote
It is recovered: the two phase flips cancel inside the block
prediction.explanation: A Z on any qubit of a block flips the sign between |000⟩ and |111⟩ in that block. Two of them flip it twice, so the block is back where it started: Z₀Z₁ is a stabilizer, and it acts as the identity on the code. The two-error failures come from other pairs, such as X on 0 and 1 (a logical Z) or Z on 0 and 3 (a logical X).

hints: Encoding has two layers, and the outer one comes first. Which three qubits form the phase-flip code, and what do you apply to them? Then each of those qubits becomes the leader of a bit-flip code on its block.

The outer layer is qml.CNOT(wires=[0, 3]), qml.CNOT(wires=[0, 6]) and a qml.Hadamard on wires 0, 3 and 6. The inner layer is, for each block (a, b, c), qml.CNOT(wires=[a, b]) and qml.CNOT(wires=[a, c]). Decoding runs the same gates in reverse order, with a Toffoli as the vote.

For each block (a, b, c), decode with qml.CNOT(wires=[a, b]), qml.CNOT(wires=[a, c]) and qml.Toffoli(wires=[b, c, a]). Then the leaders 0, 3 and 6 hold a phase-flip code: a Hadamard on each, and the same vote with qml.Toffoli(wires=[3, 6, 0]).

messages.ok: Qubit 0 is recovered after any X, Y or Z error on a single qubit, and after an arbitrary rotation on a single qubit, for every input state tested.
messages.no_circuit: Define the QNode circuit() on a default.mixed device with 9 qubits.
messages.wrong_qubits: The Shor code uses 9 qubits, but the circuit has {count}.
messages.encode_wrong: With no error at all qubit 0 does not come back to |ψ⟩ (fidelity {fidelity}). The decoding is probably not the exact reverse of the encoding: check the order of the gates in each layer.
messages.single_fail: With the error {error} qubit 0 was not recovered (fidelity {fidelity}). If only some errors fail, look at the vote that should catch them: the inner one in each block for X, the one on the leaders for Z.

challenge.mission: The Shor code corrects any one error, and the two-error buttons of the lab show that a second error can go either way: X on qubits 0 and 1 defeats the code, and so does Z on qubits 0 and 3, while X on 0 with Z on 3 does not. To see the whole picture, write survives(errors), where errors is a list of (qubit, letter) pairs with the letter "X" or "Z". It encodes a state, applies the errors, decodes with your decode(), and returns True when qubit 0 holds the input state again, whatever that state is. Then scan the pairs of qubits (0 to 8) and store three lists. In bad_xx, the pairs (i, j) with i < j for which X errors on qubits i and j defeat the code. In bad_zz, the same for two Z errors. In bad_xz, the ordered pairs (i, j) with i ≠ j for which X on qubit i and Z on qubit j defeat it. The validator calls survives on error patterns of its own, with one or two errors, and compares the three lists with its own simulation of the code.
hints: Build one QNode that takes the list of errors: prepare a state on qubit 0, call encode(), apply an X or a Z for each entry, call decode(), and return a number that says whether qubit 0 is back. For an input state, the expectation value of a Pauli operator that has that state as eigenstate is one such number.

After decoding, a failure is a Pauli operator acting on qubit 0: X or Z. X leaves |+⟩ alone and Z leaves |0⟩ alone, so a test on one of those states can miss a failure. A state that both operators change, such as the +1 eigenstate of Y, catches either.

qml.Hadamard followed by qml.S on qubit 0 prepares that state from |0⟩, and its Y expectation value is 1 when the state has survived. itertools.combinations(range(9), 2) gives the 36 unordered pairs. For bad_xz, loop over i and j separately and skip i = j.

messages.ch_ok: Two X errors defeat the code for {xx} of the 36 pairs of qubits, two Z errors for {zz} of 36, and an X on one qubit with a Z on another never does (all {xz} ordered pairs checked). The X failures all sit inside one block and the Z failures all connect two different blocks.
messages.ch_survives_error: Calling survives raised an error ({detail}). It receives a list of (qubit, letter) pairs, for example [(0, "X"), (3, "Z")], and may also receive an empty list.
messages.ch_says_survives: survives({errors}) returned True, but the code does not recover every input state after those errors. Probably the test state hides the failure: a logical X leaves |+⟩ unchanged and a logical Z leaves |0⟩ unchanged. Use a state that both change, or test more than one.
messages.ch_says_fails: survives({errors}) returned False, but the code does recover those errors. Probably an error is applied with the wrong letter or on the wrong qubit, or the fidelity is compared with a threshold that is too strict.
messages.ch_missing: Store the pairs in the variable {name}.
messages.ch_bad_format: {name} must be a list of pairs of different qubit numbers between 0 and 8, such as [(0, 1), (3, 4)].
messages.ch_listed: {name} lists the pair {pair}, but the code survives those two errors. Check that the pair is tested with the letters of this list and that survives is not too strict.
messages.ch_unlisted: {name} does not list the pair {pair}, and two such errors do break the code. Look at which test state your survives uses and whether every pair of the scan is tried.
